articles.title: PHP Dies After Every Request. How the Zend Engine Actually Runs Your Code.
articles.description: A visual, 10-minute architectural deep dive into how PHP actually executes under the hood. From the Shared-Nothing process model and OPcache bytecode caching to 16-byte zvals, Copy-on-Write, and the Tracing JIT.
articles.body_html:
For more than two decades, programmers coming from languages like Java, Python, Go, and Node.js have looked at PHP and repeated the exact same criticism:

"PHP does not even have a persistent application server. It boots up, runs a script, and dies after every single HTTP request. How could anyone build serious software on an architecture like that?"

The irony is that those critics missed the most profound design decision in modern web computing.

What looked like a primitive limitation was, in reality, a deliberate architectural choice called the Shared-Nothing Architecture.

While other language runtimes battle memory leaks that accumulate over weeks, global state that accidentally bleeds between concurrent users, and fatal unhandled exceptions that knock down entire server clusters, PHP operates on a radically different premise:

PHP executes in total isolation, reclaims every single byte of memory at the end of the request, and resets to a pristine blank slate.

Yet modern PHP is not slow. Over the last decade, the core engineering team completely rebuilt the runtime from the ground up:

  • The Zend Engine was rewritten with cache-optimized 16-byte zval structures.
  • OPcache eliminates file parsing by caching bytecode directly inside shared operating system memory.
  • Copy-on-Write ensures massive arrays consume zero extra RAM until mutated.
  • PHP 8's Tracing JIT compiles hot execution loops directly into native silicon machine code.

To truly understand why PHP powers over 75% of the web, you have to look beneath the surface syntax and examine how the Zend Engine and PHP-FPM actually execute your code under the hood.

Here is the complete journey of a PHP request.

The Shared-Nothing Philosophy: Why Dying on Purpose Is a Superpower

To appreciate the Zend Engine, you must first understand the architectural divide between long-lived persistent runtimes and PHP.

In Node.js, Python (FastAPI/Django), Ruby (Puma), and Go, your application boots once. The runtime initializes global variables, establishes database connection pools, loads framework classes, and starts an event loop or worker thread pool that lives for days or months.

This model is fast, but it carries profound architectural vulnerabilities:

  1. State Leaks Across Users: If a developer accidentally mutates a global object or attaches data to an uncleaned request context, User B can end up reading private data belonging to User A.
  2. Slow-Motion Memory Leaks: If a third-party package slowly appends items to a cache that never gets cleared, the process slowly exhausts RAM until an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer terminates the process.
  3. Catastrophic Blast Radius: If an unhandled exception causes a fatal crash or memory corruption, the entire server process dies, severing thousands of active connections simultaneously.

PHP took the opposite path: The Shared-Nothing Process Model.

When an HTTP request arrives at a PHP worker:

  1. The worker allocates a fresh, completely isolated memory arena called the Request Heap (managed by Zend Memory Manager, ZendMM).
  2. Superglobals ($_GET, $_POST, $_SERVER) are populated freshly for that specific request.
  3. Your application executes in total isolation. No other concurrent user shares that memory space.
  4. The HTTP response headers and body are flushed to the web server.
  5. The Zend Engine instantly tears down the request heap. Every variable, object, database handle, and memory buffer is wiped out in a single sweep.
  6. The worker process returns to its pristine resting state, ready for the next request.

This design gives PHP an almost indestructible reliability.

Memory leaks simply cannot survive across requests. If a buggy piece of code allocates 50 megabytes of temporary data and forgets to clean it up, the Zend Engine sweeps it away automatically the instant the response finishes.

And if a script encounters a fatal error or segmentation fault, it kills only that single worker. The master process respawns a replacement in under a millisecond without dropping any other concurrent user request.

The Compilation Pipeline: From PHP Text to Zend Opcodes

A common misconception is that because PHP dies after every request, it must re-read and re-parse your .php files from disk every time someone loads a page.

In PHP 3 and 4, that was true. In modern PHP, that model has been dead for over a decade.

When PHP processes a file, it passes through four distinct phases:

[PHP File] ──> [Lexer: Tokens] ──> [Parser: AST] ──> [Compiler: Opcodes] ──> [Zend VM Executor]

1. Lexing (Tokenization)

The Zend Lexer scans your raw PHP script and converts the character stream into a sequence of language tokens (such as T_VARIABLE, T_OBJECT_OPERATOR, T_STRING).

2. Parsing (Abstract Syntax Tree)

Introduced in PHP 7, the Zend Parser reads the tokens and constructs a hierarchical Abstract Syntax Tree (AST). The AST validates syntax, resolves operator precedence, and organizes your program logic into a structured tree before code generation.

3. Compilation (Zend Opcodes)

The compiler walks the AST and emits Zend Opcodes. An opcode is a low-level virtual machine instruction, comparable to Java bytecode or Python bytecode.

For example, this simple addition:

$c = $a + $b;

compiles into low-level instructions that look like this:

ZEND_ADD      $a, $b, ~0
ZEND_ASSIGN   $c, ~0

4. The Game Changer: OPcache in Shared Memory

In a stock PHP installation without caching, compiling source files on every request would indeed create heavy CPU overhead.

This is where OPcache enters the picture.

OPcache intercepts the compilation pipeline. The first time a PHP file is loaded, OPcache compiles it into Zend Opcodes and stores the compiled bytecode directly inside Shared Memory (SHM).

When subsequent requests arrive:

  • PHP skips the Lexer entirely.
  • PHP skips the Parser and AST construction entirely.
  • PHP skips the Compiler entirely.

Instead, the Zend VM executor fetches the pre-compiled opcodes directly from memory and executes them immediately.

With Preloading (introduced in PHP 7.4 and standard in modern frameworks like Laravel and Symfony), frameworks can compile all core classes, traits, and interfaces on server boot into permanent shared memory.

When a user request hits your application, the entire framework is already resident in RAM, ready to execute with zero initialization latency.

The 16-Byte Miracle: How the Zend Engine Stores Variables

In PHP, a variable can be an integer, a floating-point number, a string, an array, an object, or null. It can change its type dynamically at runtime:

$x = 42;
$x = "Hello World";
$x = [1, 2, 3];

How does a statically-compiled C program (which the Zend Engine is) represent a dynamically-typed variable with minimal memory overhead?

The answer is the zval (Zend Value).

In PHP 5, a zval was a bloated C structure requiring 32 to 48 bytes on 64-bit systems. Worse, every single zval was allocated as an independent block on the heap, scattering pointers across memory and causing frequent CPU cache misses.

In PHP 7, core engineer Dmitry Stogov led a complete rewrite of the Zend Engine known as phpng (PHP Next Generation). The zval was completely redesigned into an ultra-compact, 16-byte structure.

Here is what a zval looks like under the hood in C:

struct _zval_struct {
    zend_value value;            /* 8 bytes: union holding primitive or pointer */
    union {
        struct {
            zend_uchar type;     /* 1 byte: IS_LONG, IS_STRING, IS_ARRAY, etc. */
            zend_uchar type_flags;
            zend_uchar const_flags;
            zend_uchar reserved;
        } v;
        uint32_t type_info;      /* 4 bytes total */
    } u1;
    union {
        uint32_t next;           /* hash collision chaining */
        uint32_t cache_slot;     /* literal cache */
        ...
    } u2;                        /* 4 bytes total */
};

Notice the engineering elegance of this layout:

  • Exactly 16 bytes total on any 64-bit architecture.
  • For primitive integers (IS_LONG) and floats (IS_DOUBLE), the number is stored directly inside the 8-byte value field. There is zero pointer indirection and zero heap allocation!
  • For complex types like strings (IS_STRING) or arrays (IS_ARRAY), the value field stores a pointer to a dedicated payload structure (zend_string or zend_array).
  • The zval itself is allocated directly on the CPU execution stack or embedded inside contiguous array memory. It does not require separate heap allocation calls.

This single refactoring doubled PHP's raw execution speed and cut memory consumption in half across the entire world on the day PHP 7 was released.

Copy-on-Write: The Art of Memory Laziness

Consider this PHP code:

$users = get_large_user_dataset(); // A massive 100,000-item array (~20 MB)
$backup = $users;                  // What happens here?

In many languages, assigning an array to a new variable either duplicates the entire array in memory (wasting 20 MB of RAM) or passes a mutable reference where changes to $backup mutate $users.

In PHP, arrays have value semantics: modifying $backup will never mutate $users.

Does that mean PHP duplicates 20 megabytes of memory on $backup = $users?

The answer is no, thanks to Copy-on-Write (COW).

Here is how Copy-on-Write works in the Zend Engine:

  1. Assignment without Duplication: When you write $backup = $users, PHP simply copies the 16-byte zval. Both $users and $backup point to the exact same physical zend_array in memory.
  2. Refcount Increment: PHP increments the array's reference counter: gc.refcount = 2. No array data is duplicated. The operation takes mere nanoseconds.
  3. The Mutation Trigger: As long as both variables only read from the array, they share the same physical memory block forever.
  4. Physical Separation: The moment you mutate one of the variables: 
$backup[0] = "Modified User";

The Zend Engine checks the refcount. Because refcount > 1, PHP knows that multiple variables point to this memory.

Only at that exact moment does PHP clone the array in memory, allocate a fresh block for $backup, decrement $users's refcount to 1, and apply the mutation to the new clone.

If you pass a 50-megabyte array through ten functions that only read data, PHP never duplicates that array once. You get the safety of pure pass-by-value semantics with the speed and efficiency of pass-by-reference pointers.

PHP-FPM: The Resilient Worker Pool

How does a web server like Nginx or Caddy communicate with PHP in production?

The bridge is PHP-FPM (FastCGI Process Manager).

PHP does not run as an Apache module anymore. Modern production architectures run PHP as an independent daemon managing a pool of isolated worker processes.

The PHP-FPM architecture operates on a master-worker model:

  1. The Master Process: Runs as a privileged supervisor. It binds to a UNIX domain socket or TCP port, parses php.ini configurations, loads OPcache into shared memory, and spawns worker processes.
  2. The Worker Pool: A collection of pre-forked worker processes that listen for incoming FastCGI connections.
  3. Request Distribution: When Nginx receives an HTTP request for a .php endpoint, it translates the request into binary FastCGI frames and forwards it over the socket to an idle PHP-FPM worker.
  4. Execution and Cleanup: The worker executes the script, streams the generated HTML or JSON back to Nginx, runs its memory cleanup routines, and marks itself ready for the next request.

Fault Tolerance by Design

The real beauty of PHP-FPM is its fault isolation.

In a long-lived Node.js or Python process, if a native C extension crashes with a segmentation fault, the entire server process dies instantly. All ongoing requests for every user are abruptly dropped.

In PHP-FPM, if Worker 4104 encounters a fatal segmentation fault or exceeds its memory limit, only that single worker terminates.

The master process detects the signal, logs the crash, and spawns a brand new worker in fractions of a millisecond. None of the other workers are affected, and no other users experience downtime.

PHP 8's Tracing JIT: Compiling Bytecode to Native Silicon

With PHP 8, the language took its biggest evolutionary leap since PHP 7: the introduction of a Just-In-Time (JIT) Compiler.

In standard execution, the Zend VM is an interpreter. It runs an infinite loop in C that fetches an opcode, looks up the opcode handler in a table, and executes it:

while (1) {
    execute(opline++);
}

While this interpreter loop is heavily optimized, it still incurs CPU overhead: jumping through handler tables and maintaining VM stack frames.

The PHP 8 JIT bypasses this interpreter loop for performance-critical code.

PHP 8 implements a Tracing JIT:

  1. Profile Recording: As the Zend VM executes opcodes, the JIT monitors frequently executed code paths (known as hot loops or hot traces).
  2. Intermediate Representation: When an opcode sequence exceeds a designated execution threshold, the JIT records the exact type profile of the variables involved.
  3. Native Assembly Generation: Using DynASM (the assembler library originally created for LuaJIT), the JIT translates those opcodes directly into raw machine instructions: x86-64 or ARM64 assembly.
  4. Direct Execution: On subsequent iterations, the CPU executes the machine code directly on physical hardware, completely bypassing the Zend VM interpreter loop.

For typical I/O-bound web applications waiting on database queries, the JIT provides modest gains (around 5% to 15%), because database latency dominates execution time.

However, for CPU-bound tasks like image manipulation, mathematical modeling, JSON parsing, and machine learning inference, the JIT allows PHP to run at speeds approaching native C.

The Paradigm Shift: Why the Architecture Won

PHP's reputation as a "messy" language was earned in the late 1990s when developers mixed raw SQL directly into HTML templates.

Yet while developer trends have cycled through countless runtimes, frameworks, and deployment paradigms, PHP has quietly remained the workhorse of the internet.

Why? Because its core architectural philosophy was right all along:

  1. Shared-Nothing means bulletproof reliability. No memory leaks across requests, no cross-user state pollution, and instant crash isolation.
  2. OPcache delivers compiled-language speed. Source files are compiled once into shared memory, eliminating disk I/O and parsing overhead.
  3. The 16-byte zval maximizes cache locality. Small primitives never touch the heap, keeping CPU caches full and latency low.
  4. Copy-on-Write provides safety without waste. You get clean pass-by-value semantics without duplicating memory blocks.
  5. PHP-FPM scales effortlessly. Pre-forked worker pools map cleanly to multi-core servers without complex multi-threading bugs.

PHP does not survive despite its execution model. It thrives because of it.

By accepting that every request is an ephemeral, isolated event, PHP achieved what long-lived runtimes still struggle to guarantee: effortless scalability, rock-solid stability, and a developer experience where you never have to restart the server to see your code run.

When you look at modern PHP through the lens of the Zend Engine, what was the biggest revelation that changed your perspective on how the language actually works? And how do you see the balance between shared-nothing runtimes and persistent app servers evolving?

References:

  • PHP Internals Handbook: The Zend Engine & zval Architecture
  • PHP Official Documentation: OPcache & Preloading Configuration
  • Dmitry Stogov: phpng Architectural Proposal and Implementation
  • PHP RFC: JIT Compilation in PHP 8
  • Nikita Popov: Internal Memory Management in PHP 7 and 8

articles.title: Microserver Updated with Mini Catbot! ✨😻 mew!
articles.description: View mini Catbot Live: mew!      Sunday Funday... Updated my server hub which had been snoozing for a...
articles.body_html:
View mini Catbot Live: mew!

Sunday Funday... Updated my server hub which had been snoozing for a bit. The page was screaming AI-created and it was bothering me. I finally had a second to sit with it and make it feel a little bit more me-like. I get paid $0 for doing stuff like this, and I do it for pure entertainment value.

Sometimes in life, there is a point where you realize it is much faster to drop in a vector graphic, than try to reinvent the whole damn thing with CSS. Don't get me wrong, I love CSS, but I had a plan, and it absolutely had to happen.

The first part of my plan was to have blacklights casting onto to page content. I soon realized that the best placement for them was horizontally and shining down. But, before I could place my blacklights, I had to have my graphic. Generally, I am not satisfied with clipart and stock. I want my own thing, because apparently I am a digital brat.

So I chose the fast method of finding reference images of the exact blacklight I had in mind and giving them to Gemini to produce a mockup starting point. After A few renditions, I got something workable. I took that version and dropped it in illustrator, where I vectorized it using outlines and tweaked to taste. I nearly ended up with a whole damn schematic of blacklights and scaffolding.

Rabbit holes are so easy to fall into. Anyways, happy with my new creation, I used it as my blacklight on the page, and mounted it snuggly to the ceiling with some scaffolding. Perfect.

Then it was time to turn the lights on. That was a little bit of css-figuring that involved gradients and placement via percent. This could have also been a rabbit hole, but this is enough for now. 🤣 After I got the lights appearing properly, I realized it would be WAY COOLER to have a button. So I made a fun button that toggles the blacklights on and off, which also alters how the text and borders appear on the page.

And then I realized... I have a purrfect platform for a mini catbot to walk across! 🤣✨ So, having the full scale catbot at my disposal, I used claude to generate a 'mini catbot'. Mini Catbot will follow your cursor above the scaffolding, bat at the power button, and meow. And of course I updated some of the content which also served as a reminder I have more work to do. No homework or studying today... just 'fuzzacating' LOL

Claude handled the simple animation very well, I cannot take credit for that. But I do absolutely love it. ✨

Now my page feels much better! 😹

articles.title: Designing Fault-Tolerant API Through Idempotency
articles.description: So imagine I’m reading your post. I click Like, the heart turns red, and the request times out. My...
articles.body_html:
So imagine I’m reading your post. I click Like, the heart turns red, and the request times out. My frontend’s retry logic sends it again.

This time, the success reply arrives. The heart turns grey.
I know I liked your post. But your code apparently has other plans because its not FAULT TOLERANT.

Fault tolerance is an application’s ability to keep working correctly when part of the system fails. Retrying can help us recover from a temporary connection failure, but our API has to handle the second attempt safely.

For database writes, there’s a catch. Saving the change and delivering the HTTP response are separate steps. The connection can drop after the database commits, leaving the client unsure whether the write succeeded.

Let’s follow that click through MongoDB and PostgreSQL on Neon, then make the retry safe in both.

One click became two requests

Our endpoint is POST /posts/42/toggle-like. It reverses the current state. If my like exists, remove it. Otherwise, create it.

Here’s how one click manages to do both.

  1. The API saves my like.
  2. The connection drops before the success reply reaches my browser.
  3. The browser retries.
  4. The API finds the like and removes it. This reply arrives successfully.

The first write succeeded. Only its reply was lost.

The retry recovered from the connection failure, but it also reversed the user’s action. Making this endpoint fault tolerant means handling both parts correctly.

Our like can live in a MongoDB document or a PostgreSQL row on Neon. Either database will execute a fresh request to remove it. Our API told it to toggle, and it followed the instruction.

Could we wrap the toggle in a transaction?

Yes. A transaction groups database changes so they all commit together or all roll back. That’s atomicity. MongoDB supports transactions across documents on replica sets and sharded clusters. Neon supports PostgreSQL transactions. MongoDB transactions · PostgreSQL transactions

In our example, though, the first transaction already committed before the reply disappeared. The retry starts a new transaction and reverses the like.

Both transactions succeed. I’ve now unliked your post with excellent data integrity.

A row lock also ends when its transaction finishes, leaving the later retry free to make another change. PostgreSQL row locks

We need to change what repeating the request does.

Make the request say what I mean

Instead of asking the API to toggle, ask it to make sure my like exists.

The first request creates it. The retry finds it and leaves it there.

That’s idempotency; repeating the request has the same intended effect as sending it once. The responses can differ while the intended effect stays the same.

We can use PUT /posts/42/like to ensure the like exists. For an unlike, DELETE /posts/42/like ensures the like is absent.

The handler’s database operation must implement that promise. Changing the HTTP verb alone leaves the original toggle behaviour in place.

MongoDB can create a missing like with an upsert. PostgreSQL on Neon can use INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. Both need a unique rule for the user-and-post pair so simultaneous requests also produce one like.

Implementation examples

MongoDB

Create the unique index once. Then use the upsert in the request handler, taking userId from the signed-in session.

// One-time setup
await likes.createIndex(
  { postId: 1, userId: 1 },
  { unique: true }
);

// In the PUT handler
await likes.updateOne(
  { postId, userId },
  { $setOnInsert: { likedAt: new Date() } },
  { upsert: true }
);

An existing like keeps its original timestamp.

PostgreSQL on Neon

Give the likes table a primary key on (post_id, user_id), then run this parameterised query.

INSERT INTO likes (post_id, user_id)
VALUES ($1, $2)
ON CONFLICT (post_id, user_id) DO NOTHING;

The retry finds the existing pair and leaves it alone.

If you keep a separate like counter, increase it only when a new like was inserted, in the same transaction.

What if I need to keep the toggle endpoint?

The PUT approach above repeats the same desired state. If we keep POST /posts/42/toggle-like, we need a way to recognise that a particular action already happened.

Give each deliberate click an idempotency key. This key identifies one action across all its retries. The client reuses it when retrying and generates a new key for a new deliberate click.

In one transaction, claim the key under a unique constraint scoped to the user and endpoint, apply the toggle, and save its result. When the same key comes back, return the saved result.

Now test the exact failure. Let the write succeed, drop its HTTP reply, and retry. There should still be one like when you refresh.

Whether the like lives in MongoDB or Neon, both attempts now leave us with the result we wanted. One click. One like.

So if I liked your post. The heart should stay red 😂.
I hope this helps you and can guide in making your code

Thanks for reading 👍

articles.title: Building a free AI UI builder on Cloudflare: what small models taught me
articles.description: A 2 days ago I launched openconstructor, a free, open-source browser editor: you describe an...
articles.body_html:
A 2 days ago I launched openconstructor, a free, open-source browser editor: you describe an interface, an AI builds it on a canvas, and you keep editing by hand or ask the AI to change one part. It got 562 visitors in its first two days with no ads.

The whole thing runs on a Cloudflare Worker, Supabase and free open models. Here are the parts that turned out more interesting than I expected.

1. Small free models can't design, so I stopped asking them to

The built-in AI runs on open models (GPT-OSS 120B, Llama 3.3 70B) through Workers AI. They write valid HTML, but ask for an "award-winning cinematic website" and you get something different every time: sometimes great, often a plain hero and three cards.

Prompt engineering got me maybe 20% further. What worked was splitting the job:

  • the design is a set of hand-made sections (hero with a CSS 3D object, scroll-lit statement, services, case studies, logo wall…);
  • the model only writes the content, as JSON. 
// the model gets a schema with defaults and returns only this
{
  "brand": "Ember", "hue": 28,
  "titleA": "Roasted by fire.", "titleB": "Poured with care.",
  "services": [["Roast", "Small batches on a 1960s drum roaster."], ...],
  "heroArt": "amber neon cube over dark sand dunes, cinematic 3d render"
}

The page is then assembled from the sections. hue rotates the template's accent colours, so a coffee roaster gets amber and an AI lab gets violet. Same model, but the result went from "sometimes nice" to consistently polished, in about 6 seconds.

Lesson: with weak models, move the taste into code and let the model fill in the blanks.

2. Published pages run zero JavaScript

Users publish pages to openconstructor.pw/p/<name>. Since anyone can publish, every page is served with:

Content-Security-Policy: sandbox allow-forms ...; script-src 'none'

No scripts at all. So how do pages still feel alive? Modern CSS covers more than I thought:

@supports (animation-timeline: view()) {
  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
    .section {
      animation: rise linear both;
      animation-timeline: view();
      animation-range: entry 0% cover 30%;
    }
  }
}
@keyframes rise { from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(64px); } }

Scroll-driven animations, perspective + preserve-3d for floating 3D objects, marquees with mask fades: all without a single line of JS. Browsers without support just show the content.

3. Screenshots without a server

The sandbox has a side effect: the page has an opaque origin, so the gallery can't measure or screenshot it in an iframe. Headless Chrome on the server would be costly.

Instead, the editor takes the screenshot itself at publish time:

  1. lay the page out in a hidden iframe to measure its height;
  2. put the HTML into an SVG <foreignObject>;
  3. draw that SVG onto a <canvas> and export JPEG. 
const svg = `<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="${w}" height="${h}">
  <foreignObject width="100%" height="100%">${xhtml}</foreignObject></svg>`;
img.src = 'data:image/svg+xml,' + encodeURIComponent(svg);
ctx.drawImage(img, 0, 0);
canvas.toBlob(upload, 'image/jpeg', 0.82);

The worker stores two images in KV: a 1200×630 one for link previews (og:image) and a full-page one for the gallery, which scrolls through it on hover. About 40 KB each.

4. My biggest mistake: a sign-up wall I didn't notice

After launch I looked at the numbers: hundreds of visitors, two accounts. It turned out the free AI required signing in. So most people opened the editor, typed a prompt and hit a login form.

Now visitors get 3 free generations a day without an account (counted in KV per hashed IP, the IP itself isn't stored). An account gives 20 a day, cloud projects and publishing. A friendly offer appears after the first good result, not before.

Lesson: test your product signed out, in a private window, before every launch post.

Try it / read the code

  • Live: https://openconstructor.pw
  • Code: https://github.com/Kuloka/openconstructor

It also exports to React, Vue, Svelte and even Roblox UI and LÖVE 2D. I'd love feedback, especially on where the AI output falls apart.

articles.title: How to make Vue Dynamic Components more stable
articles.description: Hey Folks, it's me again!  Today, I would like to share with you how I recently made the Vue Dynamic...
articles.body_html:
Hey Folks, it's me again!

Today, I would like to share with you how I recently made the Vue Dynamic Components bit more stable to avoid unexpected cases, improve props stability, and in general provide better developer experience.

This is how I solved my problem, if you encounter the same and you solved it differently, please let me know in the comments! :)

Problem

The default Vue Dynamic Components definitely gives you a lot of flexibility but to my taste a bit too much - especially if you want to have a better Type Safety with TypeScript. Let's take a look at the following example:

<script>
import { ref } from 'vue';
import AwesomeButton from './AwesomeButton.vue';

const shouldDisplayButton = ref(true);
</script>

<template>
  <div>
    <component
      :is="shouldDisplayButton ? 'AsewomeButton' : 'div'"
      @click="console.log('Hello World')"
      :text="Click me"
    ></component>
  </div>
</template>

There are two problems here:

  1. The prop is accepts either a string or an actual Vue component - which makes it easy have unexpected and sometimes difficult to track bugs (in the example, I made a typo 'AsewomeButton' instead of 'AwesomeButton'
  2. There is no typechecking for the props that are passed to this dynamic component which can result in a div receiving text and @click handler.

These problems can be difficult to track as the linter, compiler or TS check could miss them as technically they are correct.

Solution

We first tried with the Eslint rule that would forbid having a regular string in :is but this didn't solve our problem of props so we decided to create our wrapper abstraction over native Vue <component :is> that looks more or less like following:

import { h } from 'vue'
import type { Component, NativeElements, SetupContext, VNode } from 'vue'

type NativeTag = keyof NativeElements

type ComponentProps<C> = C extends new (...args: never[]) => {
  $props: infer P
}
  ? Omit<NonNullable<P>, 'is'>
  : C extends (props: infer P, ...args: never[]) => unknown
    ? Omit<P, 'is'>
    : Record<string, unknown>

type DynamicProps<C> = C extends NativeTag
  ? NativeElements[C]
  : ComponentProps<C>

// The `Component` type says nothing about props, so none could be checked.
type SpecificComponent<T> = Component extends T
  ? 'Type `is` as a specific component, not as `Component`'
  : unknown

export type DynamicComponentProps<T extends NativeTag | Component> = {
  is: T & SpecificComponent<T>
} & DynamicProps<T>

export function DynamicComponent<T extends NativeTag | Component>(
  props: DynamicComponentProps<T>,
  { slots }: Pick<SetupContext, 'slots'>,
): VNode {
  const { is, ...rest } = props
  return h(is, rest, slots)
}

DynamicComponent.inheritAttrs = false

There is a bunch of code so let me explain below what most important parts of it does:

NativeTag

There might be cases where the ternary would result in native HTML tag and that we don't want to forbid. So scenario like :is="'div'" should still be allowed.

ComponentProps & DynamicProps

We want to typecheck the passed component and dynamic props as a union of ternary elements. So if we expect that this dynamic component can be either X or Y, the only possible passable props should be the ones that are common for both X & Y.

SpecificComponent

What shouldn't be allowed is this: :is="'AwesomeComponent'"(passed as a string). This though should be possible :is="AwesomeComponent"

DynamicComponent

We use the Vue render function to render this component. For the users, the usage will be almost the same as the native Vue dynamic component - the only thing we replace is <component> with `' (to avoid name collisions).

Summary

This helped us discovered few cases that were working but were really error prone (a typo would break the page/component). We also have a rule that disalows usage of :is that results to string that is not native html tag, and also prompts the developer to use DynamicComponent instead. This way we advocate this more safer and stable solution to other devs.

Let me know how you are solving similar problems! :)

articles.title: TypeScript `Map` and `Set` Iteration in 2026: Why `downlevelIteration` Still Breaks Production Builds
articles.description: The downlevelIteration flag controls how TypeScript transpiles Map, Set, and array iteration to older JavaScript. Production builds still break without it because the default transpilation produces index-based loops that fail on iterables. Here's wha
articles.body_html:
TypeScript Map and Set Iteration in 2026: Why downlevelIteration Still Breaks Production Builds

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

TypeScript's downlevelIteration flag determines how the compiler transpiles Map, Set, and array iteration when targeting older JavaScript runtimes. Without it, production builds silently produce broken code that crashes on iterables at runtime. The default behavior downlevels for...of loops to index-based iteration, which fails on objects that implement Symbol.iterator but lack numeric indices.

The flag's confusing name compounds the problem. Developers expect "downlevel" to mean "produce simpler code for older targets," but enabling the flag actually generates more complex helper code that checks for Symbol.iterator before falling back to index-based iteration. The flag appears optional until a production build crashes with "Object is not iterable" on a perfectly valid Map.values() call.

Problem flowchart showing downlevelIteration false leading to index-based iteration that crashes on Map

The correct configuration enables downlevelIteration when targeting runtimes below ES2015 and using Map, Set, or any iterable protocol. The transpiled output includes a __values helper that tests for Symbol.iterator support before attempting iteration. This prevents the crash but increases bundle size by 400-800 bytes per file that uses iteration.

Solution flowchart showing downlevelIteration true generating helper code that handles iterables correctly

Key Takeaways

  • The downlevelIteration flag controls whether TypeScript emits index-based loops or iterator-protocol-aware helpers when transpiling iteration to ES5 or earlier.
  • Without downlevelIteration, for...of loops on Map, Set, or any Symbol.iterator object crash at runtime because the default transpilation assumes numeric indices.
  • TypeScript 6.0 deprecated target: es5, but builds targeting ES2015+ still encounter iteration failures in polyfilled environments where iterables exist but the target is set to ES5 for legacy browser support.
  • Enabling downlevelIteration adds 400-800 bytes per file but prevents runtime crashes when iterating Map, Set, array spreads, or destructuring iterables.
  • The flag name misleads developers into thinking it produces simpler code for older targets, when it actually generates more sophisticated helpers that respect the iteration protocol.

What downlevelIteration Actually Does (And Why the Name Confuses Everyone)

TypeScript's terminology inverts the intuitive meaning of "downlevel." The flag name suggests producing simpler code, but downlevelIteration: true emits more complex helpers that implement ES2015 iteration semantics in ES5 environments.

When targeting ES5 or earlier, TypeScript must transpile iteration primitives introduced in ES2015: for...of loops, array spreads ([...arr]), argument spreads (fn(...args)), and destructuring iterables. The default behavior produces index-based loops that fail on objects implementing Symbol.iterator.

const map = new Map([['a', 1], ['b', 2]]);
for (const [key, value] of map) {
  console.log(key, value);
}

Without downlevelIteration, this transpiles to:

var map = new Map([['a', 1], ['b', 2]]);
for (var _i = 0, map_1 = map; _i < map_1.length; _i++) {
  var _a = map_1[_i], key = _a[0], value = _a[1];
  console.log(key, value);
}

The transpiled code accesses map.length and map[0], which do not exist on Map objects. The loop never executes. Runtime engines that support Map but run ES5 code produce no error and no output, silently skipping the iteration. Older engines that lack Map entirely throw "Map is not defined," but that failure occurs earlier during Map construction, masking the iteration problem.

TypeScript downlevelIteration flag configuration example

With downlevelIteration: true, TypeScript emits a __values helper that checks for Symbol.iterator before falling back to index-based iteration:

var __values = (this && this.__values) || function(o) {
  var s = typeof Symbol === "function" && Symbol.iterator, m = s && o[s], i = 0;
  if (m) return m.call(o);
  if (o && typeof o.length === "number") return {
    next: function () {
      if (o && i >= o.length) o = void 0;
      return { value: o && o[i++], done: !o };
    }
  };
  throw new TypeError(s ? "Object is not iterable." : "Symbol.iterator is not defined.");
};

var map = new Map([['a', 1], ['b', 2]]);
try {
  for (var map_1 = __values(map), map_1_1 = map_1.next(); !map_1_1.done; map_1_1 = map_1.next()) {
    var _a = map_1_1.value, key = _a[0], value = _a[1];
    console.log(key, value);
  }
} catch (e_1_1) { e_1 = { error: e_1_1 }; }
finally {
  try {
    if (map_1_1 && !map_1_1.done && (_a = map_1.return)) _a.call(map_1);
  }
  finally { if (e_1) throw e_1.error; }
}

The helper first tests whether Symbol.iterator exists on the object. If present, it calls the iterator method and consumes the result. If absent, it falls back to numeric indexing. The transpiled loop now respects the iteration protocol, correctly iterating Map entries.

The confusion arises because "downlevel" typically means "produce simpler code for older targets." Enabling downlevelIteration does the opposite: it produces more sophisticated code that handles both iterable and array-like objects. The flag should have been named strictIteration or iteratorHelpers, but the existing name persists in TypeScript 6.0 despite the ES5 target deprecation.

Concept diagram showing how downlevelIteration transforms iteration to check Symbol.iterator before falling back to index-based loops

Map and Set Iteration Without the Flag: The Silent Breakage

The runtime failure mode depends on the JavaScript engine and the transpilation target. Modern engines that support Map and Set execute the broken code without throwing errors. The iteration simply skips all entries, producing silent bugs that pass unit tests running on modern runtimes but fail in production on older browsers.

A production application targeting ES5 for IE11 compatibility experiences the failure when deployed:

const permissions = new Set(['read', 'write', 'delete']);
const granted = [...permissions];
console.log(granted);

Without downlevelIteration, the spread operator transpiles to:

var permissions = new Set(['read', 'write', 'delete']);
var granted = [].concat(permissions);
console.log(granted);

The Array.prototype.concat method expects array-like objects or primitives. When passed a Set, it treats the entire Set as a single element. The output is [Set(3)], not ['read', 'write', 'delete']. The code executes without errors, but the result is wrong.

Unit tests running on Node.js 20 or Chrome 120 pass because those environments execute the original TypeScript source through transpilation pipelines that default to ES2020+ targets. The test suite never exercises the ES5 transpilation. The bug only appears when the production build runs on the intended target runtime.

Map and Set iteration failure visualization

The for...of loop failure is harder to detect because the loop body never executes. Developers writing iteration logic for Map or Set assume the loop will run at least once if the collection is non-empty. When the transpiled code silently skips all entries, downstream logic that depends on the iteration produces unexpected results without obvious stack traces pointing to the iteration site.

A real-world example from an e-commerce checkout flow:

const lineItems = new Map<string, number>();
lineItems.set('item-123', 2);
lineItems.set('item-456', 1);

let total = 0;
for (const [id, quantity] of lineItems) {
  const price = getPriceById(id);
  total += price * quantity;
}

if (total === 0) {
  throw new Error('Cart is empty');
}

Without downlevelIteration, the for...of loop never executes. The total remains 0, and the code throws "Cart is empty" even though the lineItems map contains entries. The error message misleads the developer into investigating cart state management when the actual bug is transpilation configuration.

The destructuring assignment inside the loop exacerbates the failure. The transpiled code attempts to destructure map_1[_i], which is undefined. Older engines throw "Cannot read property '0' of undefined," providing a clearer diagnostic. Modern engines that support destructuring but execute the ES5 transpilation produce the same error, but the stack trace points to the transpiled output, not the original source, complicating debugging.

For a detailed comparison of how TypeScript handles readonly collections, see the ReadonlyMap and ReadonlySet in TypeScript post.

TypeScript 6.0 Changes: Why This Flag Still Matters After ES5 Deprecation

TypeScript 6.0 deprecated target: es5, making ES2015 the minimum supported target. The deprecation does not eliminate the need for downlevelIteration because production builds still target ES5 through external tooling or continue using the deprecated target with a suppression flag.

Configuration scenario downlevelIteration requirement Reason
TypeScript 6.0 with target: es2015 or higher Not required Native for...of and Symbol.iterator available in target runtime
TypeScript 6.0 with target: es5 (deprecated) Required if using Map, Set, or iterables Transpilation still produces index-based loops without the flag
TypeScript 5.x with target: es5 Required if using Map, Set, or iterables No deprecation; standard configuration
External compiler (Babel, SWC) with ES5 target Depends on external tool TypeScript does not control final output; Babel and SWC handle iteration independently

The deprecation warning reads:

Option 'target: es5' is deprecated and will stop functioning in a future release. Use 'target: es2015' or higher.

Projects that suppress the warning by adding "ignoreDeprecations": "5.0" to tsconfig.json continue using target: es5 in TypeScript 6.0. The transpilation behavior remains identical to TypeScript 5.x. The downlevelIteration flag still determines whether iteration produces index-based loops or iterator-aware helpers.

External compilers introduce another dimension. A common build pipeline uses TypeScript for type checking only ("noEmit": true) and Babel or SWC for transpilation. These tools handle iteration independently:

Comparison flowchart showing TypeScript 6.0 with target es5 vs. target es2015 handling of downlevelIteration

Babel's @babel/preset-env transpiles iteration based on the targets configuration, not TypeScript's target. When targets includes ES5 browsers, Babel emits its own iteration helpers regardless of downlevelIteration. SWC behaves similarly, using its jsc.target option to determine transpilation.

A mixed configuration causes confusion:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2015",
    "downlevelIteration": false
  }
}

TypeScript emits ES2015 code with native for...of loops. Babel then transpiles to ES5, producing index-based loops that fail on iterables. The developer expects downlevelIteration: false to be safe because the TypeScript target is ES2015, but the final output still breaks.

The solution requires aligning TypeScript's target with the final output target. When using external transpilers, set TypeScript's target to match the highest version the pipeline supports before external transpilation. For type-checking-only workflows, set target: esnext and let the external tool handle all transpilation.

The TypeScript team's recommendation in the 6.0 release notes suggests using external compilers for ES5 output rather than fighting the deprecated target: es5 option. This shifts the iteration problem to Babel or SWC configuration but does not eliminate it. Developers still need to understand how iteration transpiles to ES5 to configure the external tool correctly.

Real-World Build Failures: Spread Operators, for...of, and Destructuring

Production failures cluster around three iteration primitives: spread operators, for...of loops, and destructuring assignments. Each fails differently when downlevelIteration is disabled and the target is ES5.

Array spreads produce wrong results without throwing errors:

const base = [1, 2, 3];
const extended = [0, ...base, 4];

Without downlevelIteration, this transpiles to:

var base = [1, 2, 3];
var extended = [0].concat(base, [4]);

For arrays, concat works correctly. The problem appears when spreading non-array iterables:

const uniqueIds = new Set(['a', 'b', 'c']);
const idArray = [...uniqueIds];

The transpiled code uses concat:

var uniqueIds = new Set(['a', 'b', 'c']);
var idArray = [].concat(uniqueIds);

The result is [Set(3)], not ['a', 'b', 'c']. The spread operator treats the entire Set as one element.

Destructuring assignments fail silently on Map.entries():

const config = new Map([['timeout', 5000], ['retries', 3]]);
const [[timeoutKey, timeoutValue]] = config;

The transpiled code accesses config[0]:

var config = new Map([['timeout', 5000], ['retries', 3]]);
var _a = config[0], timeoutKey = _a[0], timeoutValue = _a[1];

The expression config[0] is undefined. Destructuring undefined throws "Cannot read property '0' of undefined." The error message does not mention Map or iteration, obscuring the root cause.

Practical flowchart showing three iteration primitives and their failure modes without downlevelIteration

A production case from a logging pipeline:

const logLevels = new Set(['error', 'warn', 'info']);
const filters = [...logLevels].map(level => `level:${level}`);

Without downlevelIteration, filters becomes ["[object Set]"] instead of ["level:error", "level:warn", "level:info"]. The logging query breaks, filtering out all logs because the filter string does not match any actual log level.

The for...of failure affects React applications that iterate Map state:

const [items, setItems] = useState(new Map());

return (
  <ul>
    {Array.from(items).map(([id, item]) => (
      <li key={id}>{item.name}</li>
    ))}
  </ul>
);

When transpiled to ES5 without downlevelIteration, the Array.from call fails because items[Symbol.iterator] does not exist in the transpiled output's mental model. The component renders an empty list even when items contains entries.

The Biome linter detects some iteration patterns that require downlevelIteration, but the check is not comprehensive. For more on Biome's capabilities, see the Biome vs. oxlint Comparison in 2026 post.

Migration Strategy: When to Enable It and What Breaks When You Don't

Enabling downlevelIteration requires evaluating the tradeoff between bundle size and correctness. The flag adds 400-800 bytes per file that uses iteration, depending on how many iteration primitives appear in the source.

A migration strategy starts with identifying files that iterate Map, Set, or non-array iterables. Grep the codebase for for...of, spread operators, and destructuring:

grep -rn "for (const .* of" src/
grep -rn "\.\.\." src/
grep -rn "const \[.*\] =" src/

Files that iterate only arrays do not require downlevelIteration. The default index-based transpilation works correctly for arrays because they have numeric indices and a length property.

Migration flowchart showing decision tree for when to enable downlevelIteration

For projects using target: es5 in TypeScript 6.0, enable downlevelIteration immediately. The bundle size increase is unavoidable when correctness depends on iteration over non-array iterables.

For projects using external transpilers, the configuration depends on the tool:

Babel with @babel/preset-env:

{
  "presets": [
    ["@babel/preset-env", {
      "targets": { "ie": "11" },
      "useBuiltIns": "usage",
      "corejs": 3
    }]
  ]
}

Babel's useBuiltIns: usage option automatically includes the iteration helpers when the source code uses iteration primitives. The TypeScript downlevelIteration setting has no effect because Babel performs the transpilation.

SWC with jsc.target: es5:

{
  "jsc": {
    "target": "es5",
    "loose": false
  }
}

SWC's loose: false setting emits strict iteration helpers that respect Symbol.iterator. Setting loose: true produces simpler but incorrect transpilation that assumes all iterables are arrays.

A hybrid approach splits the codebase. Modules that use Map or Set enable downlevelIteration via a separate tsconfig.json:

{
  "extends": "./tsconfig.base.json",
  "compilerOptions": {
    "downlevelIteration": true
  },
  "include": ["src/collections/**/*"]
}

The base configuration keeps downlevelIteration: false, reducing bundle size for modules that iterate only arrays. The build pipeline compiles both configurations and merges the output.

For correlation ID propagation patterns across async boundaries, which often involve iteration over trace contexts, see the Correlation IDs for AI Agent Tracing post.

The most pragmatic approach for new projects in 2026 is to avoid the problem entirely by setting target: es2015 or higher. Modern browsers that support Map and Set also support native iteration. Legacy browser support increasingly relies on polyfills for missing APIs rather than transpiling syntax. The downlevelIteration flag becomes irrelevant when the target runtime includes Symbol.iterator natively.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does enabling downlevelIteration affect projects that do not use Map or Set?

Enabling downlevelIteration when iterating only arrays has minimal impact. The __values helper checks for Symbol.iterator and falls back to index-based iteration when absent, producing the same behavior as the default transpilation. The cost is the helper function's bundle size, typically 400-600 bytes per file.

Can I use downlevelIteration with target es2015 or higher?

Yes, but the flag has no effect when the target runtime natively supports Symbol.iterator. TypeScript emits native for...of loops and spread operators when target: es2015 or higher, bypassing the iteration helpers entirely. The flag only matters for target: es5 or target: es3.

Why does TypeScript not enable downlevelIteration by default?

The default is false for backward compatibility and bundle size. Enabling the flag globally increases output size for all files that use iteration, even when iterating arrays. Projects that do not use Map or Set pay the bundle size cost without gaining correctness. TypeScript prioritizes smaller default output over automatic correctness in edge cases.

How do I detect iteration bugs caused by missing downlevelIteration at build time?

TypeScript's compiler does not warn when iteration fails at runtime due to missing downlevelIteration. Static analysis tools like Biome can detect some patterns, but comprehensive detection requires runtime testing on the target environment. The most reliable approach is running integration tests on the actual transpiled output in an ES5 environment like IE11 or a headless browser configured to ES5 mode.

What happens when downlevelIteration is enabled but Symbol.iterator is not polyfilled?

The __values helper checks for Symbol.iterator at runtime. If absent, it falls back to index-based iteration, producing the same behavior as downlevelIteration: false for iterables. The difference is the helper throws a clear error ("Symbol.iterator is not defined") instead of silently failing. For Map and Set, the runtime must polyfill those constructors separately; downlevelIteration only handles the iteration protocol.

Conclusion: The One tsconfig Flag That Still Haunts Production Deployments

The downlevelIteration flag remains a frequent source of production bugs in 2026 despite ES5 target deprecation. Projects using Map, Set, or any Symbol.iterator implementation must enable the flag when transpiling to ES5, regardless of whether TypeScript or an external tool performs the transpilation. The default behavior produces index-based loops that fail silently on iterables, causing wrong results that pass unit tests on modern runtimes but break in production on legacy browsers.

TypeScript 6.0's ES5 deprecation shifts the problem to external compilers but does not eliminate it. Developers must understand how iteration transpiles across the entire build pipeline, from TypeScript's type checking through Babel or SWC's final output. The bundle size cost of 400-800 bytes per file is unavoidable when correctness depends on iteration over non-array collections.

For new projects, setting target: es2015 or higher avoids the flag entirely by relying on native iteration support in modern runtimes. Legacy browser support increasingly uses polyfills for missing APIs rather than transpiling syntax. The downlevelIteration flag becomes a legacy configuration option, relevant only to projects maintaining IE11 compatibility or transpiling to truly ancient JavaScript runtimes.
